title: Opiate addictiveness may derive from an ancient role in keeping cells together

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Opiate addictiveness may derive from an ancient role in keeping cells together

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: If multicellularity arose from a drive to minimize predictive error, cells need a way to keep other cells nearby; this suggests the testable hypothesis that the addictive power of opiates and similar molecules derives from such ancient roots, which could be tested in early models of multicellularity and stem/somatic cell co-cultures.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Levin M 2019, The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition › Predictions and Research Program

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Specifically, the implementation of multicellularity by the drive to minimize predictive error (Fields and Levin, 2019) suggests that cells need a way to keep other cells nearby. This suggests the testable hypothesis that the addictive power of opiates and similar molecules derives from such ancient roots.

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Levin M, “The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition”, Frontiers in psychology (2019), doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2019.02688; section “Predictions and Research Program”. Scope: Opioid and addiction-related signalling in early multicellular models and cell co-cultures

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on levin-2019-boundary-27: needs-new-data, resolvability 0.38

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The hypothesis can be made testable through defined adhesion and preference phenotypes, but the crucial early-multicellularity experiments are not represented by known public datasets. Existing pharmacology and sequence data provide context rather than a decisive test.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: In early multicellular models and stem/somatic co-cultures, manipulate opioid signaling and measure stable aggregation, separation costs, and repeated preference, then compare evolutionary conservation with neural reward pathways.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Existing molecular homology cannot establish the proposed ancient function.

Addictiveness has no direct equivalent in cell collectives.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The author marks this as a testable hypothesis about opioids and cell proximity in simple systems. Receptor catalogs document modern pharmacology and contain none of those aggregation measurements. A historical 'derives from' claim is only weakly tied to a future adhesion result, but the physiological prediction itself is an experiment that has not been deposited. Resolving even the weaker reading needs new assays.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: In a basal multicellular model and in stem/somatic co-cultures, measure whether opioids increase cell-cell retention or aggregation relative to receptor-blocked controls, beyond known effects on mammalian reward circuits. A retention effect in those simple systems would support the physiological half; no effect outside nervous systems would undercut the ancient-root hypothesis.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
No public co-culture or choanoflagellate dataset applies opioids and scores cell proximity.

A positive adhesion effect would still be compatible with a later co-option.

Mammalian addiction assays do not establish an ancient cell-keeping function.
